summary: Specifies the format of RDMA Connection Manager private data exchanged between RPC-over-RDMA version 1 peers when establishing a connection. It is an optional extension that does not change the version 1 protocol and updates RFC 8166.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers shake hands, they can pass a little extra note. This says what the note looks like.

questions: how do rpc-over-rdma peers exchange connection details
what is remote invalidation in rdma
subtitle: A tiny handshake note that lets RPC-over-RDMA peers agree on bigger messages and remote invalidation.

tldr.problem: RPC-over-RDMA version 1 has small default message sizes and no way to use remote invalidation, and its XDR headers cannot be extended without breaking existing implementations.
tldr.mechanism: Peers exchange an 8-byte Private Data message in the RDMA Connection Manager at connection setup. It carries a format identifier, a version, a remote-invalidation flag and encoded send and receive sizes.
tldr.outcome: The exchange is optional and does not change the version 1 protocol, so peers that skip it keep working with default settings. RFC 8797 updates RFC 8166.

today: RFC 8797 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 8166.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RPC-over-RDMA version 1 (RFC 8166) moves payload data for RPC-based protocols using Remote Direct Memory Access. RFC 8797 names two shortcomings. Small default Send messages force the use of costly RDMA Read or Write operations even for small payloads, and there is no facility for remote invalidation.

The version 1 Transport Header is defined in XDR and cannot be extended while keeping interoperability with existing implementations. So the RFC uses an out-of-band approach: a simple, non-XDR message passed in the Private Data field of the RDMA transport at connection time, as in MPA or the InfiniBand Connection Manager.

Implementing the exchange is OPTIONAL, and it does not alter the XDR definition in RFC 8166.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of talking could not be changed without confusing old computers, so this adds a small side note passed when the two first connect.

sections.title: Inline Threshold Size
sections.content:
An inline threshold is the maximum number of bytes that can be sent with one RDMA Send and received with one RDMA Receive. A connection has two: client-to-server and server-to-client. If an incoming message exceeds the receiver's threshold, the Receive fails and the RDMA provider typically ends the connection. A sender therefore has to use costlier explicit RDMA data transfers for larger RPC messages.

The default is 1024 bytes, which suits nearly all NFS version 3 procedures. NFS version 4 COMPOUND operations are larger on average, which forces explicit RDMA operations for frequent requests such as LOOKUP and GETATTR. RPCSEC_GSS security also enlarges RPC messages. If both sides could agree on larger thresholds, common transactions would avoid that cost.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a mail slot that only fits small envelopes. Bigger parcels need a slower trip to the counter, so it helps if both sides agree to use a wider slot.

sections.title: Remote Invalidation
sections.content:
After an RDMA data transfer, an RDMA consumer can ask its peer's network card to invalidate the Steering Tag (STag) tied to that transfer. It does this by posting an RDMA Send with Invalidate in place of a plain Send; each one carries one STag.

If both peers support it, a responder can use this when replying to a request that supplied chunks, making finalizing the results simpler and faster. The RFC lists caveats: not all RNICs support it, not all responders can send it, not all requesters can recognize it, and a requester may mix STags that may be invalidated remotely with ones that must not be, with no RDMA-layer indication of which is which.

A responder therefore must not use it unless it knows its own stack and the requester support it. Some NFS/RDMA clients have STags that are always safe to invalidate remotely, and for them a single indication is enough.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like asking the other side to tear up the claim ticket as soon as the job is done. That is only safe if you know the other side can do it and the ticket is never needed again.

sections.title: The Private Data Message
sections.content:
When the connection is set up, the client (which actively connects) and the server (which passively accepts) both fill the Connection Manager Private Data field using the same format. The properties are fixed for the life of the connection, and an implementation MUST be prepared for them to change on reconnection. If the field is too small for the message, or the transport has no Connection Manager, the field cannot be used.

The first eight octets hold these fields:

  • Format Identifier, 32 bits: always 0xf6ab0e18 in network byte order.
  • Version, 8 bits: the value 1 means exactly eight octets are present in the order described.
  • Reserved, 7 bits: senders MUST set them to zero and receivers MUST ignore them.
  • R, 1 bit: the sender supports remote invalidation.
  • Send Size, 8 bits: the encoded maximum bytes this peer will send in one RDMA Send.
  • Receive Size, 8 bits: the encoded maximum bytes this peer will accept in one RDMA Receive.

When both peers set R, the responder MAY use RDMA Send with Invalidate for RPC Replies. Each one MUST invalidate an STag associated only with the XID in the rdma_xid field of the Transport Header it carries. If either peer clears R, the responder MUST use only plain RDMA Send for Replies.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a little form with a few boxes: a secret stamp that proves it is the right kind of note, a version number, a yes/no box for the tear-up trick, and two boxes for how big a package you can send and receive.

sections.title: Encoding Sizes
sections.content:
Inline thresholds from 1024 to 262144 octets can be represented. Because 1024 is the minimum, the field holds the number of additional kilo-octets beyond the first 1024. A sender divides its actual buffer size by 1024 and subtracts one; a receiver adds one to the encoded value and multiplies by 1024.

Each side then takes the smaller of the two relevant numbers. The client uses the smaller of its own send size and the server's reported receive size as the client-to-server threshold. The server uses the smaller of its own send size and the client's reported receive size as the server-to-client threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing a big number, each side writes how many extra chunks it can handle. Then both use whichever side's limit is smaller, so nothing gets squeezed into a slot too small.

sections.title: Interoperability Rules
sections.content:
The extension must interoperate fully with version 1 implementations that do not exchange this data, and with RDMA implementations that use Private Data for other purposes. If a peer does not receive a conforming message, it MUST behave as if the remote supports only the default RFC 8166 settings: the remote invalidation flag clear and both Size fields zero.

The Format Identifier lets implementations tell this data from other Private Data, such as that defined by MPAv2. The receiver searches the buffer for the identifier, whose offset need not be aligned. If it is absent, the receiver MUST act as if no such data was provided. If found, the receiver parses what follows, and should check that the version is recognized and that the content does not overrun the buffer.
sections.plainLanguage: If the note is missing or does not have the secret stamp, the other side just assumes the usual small settings and carries on.

sections.title: Extending the Format and the IANA Registry
sections.content:
Any future format must still interoperate with implementations that do not know it. The RFC names two routes: use a different value in the first four bytes, or keep the Format Identifier and use a Version other than one. New formats would add fields starting at byte eight or redefine bits in the Reserved field.

IANA created the "RDMA-CM Private Data Identifiers" subregistry of 32-bit numbers, with fields Format Identifier, Length, Description and Reference. Its one initial entry is 0xf6ab0e18, length 8, "RPC-over-RDMA version 1 CM Private Data", reference RFC 8797. New entries use the Specification Required policy; the Designated Expert posts requests to the NFSV4 Working Group mailing list and decides within 30 days.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone wants a new kind of note later, they need a new secret stamp number or a new version number, and they register it so nobody picks the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol relies on the Reliable Connected queue pair type, whose use ensures the integrity and source authenticity of Private Data; interference with data in transit results in the provider ending the connection. IPsec is the recommended default for generic RDMA security and protects the exchange when used with RDMAP, DDP and MPA, but it is not available for InfiniBand or RoCE, which rely on physical security and cyclic redundancy checks.

The exchange does not expose upper-layer payloads to an attacker. Setting a field wrongly can cause disconnection, a self-imposed denial of service, and the same can happen if unrelated Private Data happens to contain the Format Identifier. The extra checks described for the interoperability section reduce that risk. Documents extending the format must discuss security of any new data items.
sections.plainLanguage: The note itself does not give away any secrets. The main risk is filling it in wrong, which could make the connection drop.

fields.name: Format Identifier
fields.desc: Fixed value that marks this as RPC-over-RDMA version 1 Private Data.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Senders set to zero; receivers ignore.

fields.name: Send Size
fields.desc: Encoded maximum bytes sent in one RDMA Send.

fields.name: Receive Size
fields.desc: Encoded maximum bytes received in one RDMA Receive.
